title: Conditionals
intro: Conditional sentences have an if clause and a main clause. This guide goes from the real conditionals (zero, first and second, B1) to the unreal past (third, mixed, wishes, B2).

sources.label: British Council: Zero, first and second conditionals
British Council: Third and mixed conditionals
British Council: Wish and if only

sections.title: Zero conditional
sections.summary: Use the zero conditional for facts, rules and things that are always true.
uses: Scientific facts and rules: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
Habits and routines: If I miss the bus, I walk to work.
You can use when instead of if because the result is always the same.
Instructions with an imperative: If you feel ill, stay at home.

examples.text: If water reaches 100 degrees, it boils.
When I am tired, I go to bed early.
examples.note: Both clauses use the present simple.

examples.text: Whenever he cooks, the kitchen is a mess.

mistakes.wrong: If you will heat ice, it melts.
mistakes.right: If you heat ice, it melts.
mistakes.why: Do not use will in the if clause.

mistakes.wrong: If I will be late, I phone my mum.
mistakes.right: If I am late, I phone my mum.
mistakes.why: The zero conditional uses the present simple in both parts.

checks.question: Complete: If you ___ (press) this button, the door opens.
checks.explanation: Present simple in the if clause.

checks.question: Complete: When the sun sets, it ___ (get) cold.
checks.explanation: The result is always true, so the main clause is present simple.

sections.title: First conditional
sections.summary: Use the first conditional for real or possible situations in the future and their results.
uses: A possible future situation and its likely result.
A warning, a promise or an offer: If you touch it, you will get hurt.
The if clause can come first or second. Use a comma only when the if clause comes first.
Unless means if not: Unless you hurry, you will miss the train.

examples.text: If I see Anna, I will tell her.
We won't go out if it snows.
What will you do if you don't get the job?

mistakes.wrong: If it will rain, I will take an umbrella.
mistakes.right: If it rains, I will take an umbrella.
mistakes.why: Do not use will in the if clause.

mistakes.wrong: If I will see him, I tell him.
mistakes.right: If I see him, I will tell him.
mistakes.why: The if clause uses the present simple. The main clause uses will.

checks.question: Complete: If she ___ (come), we will start.
checks.explanation: The if clause uses the present simple.

checks.question: Complete: If you heat ice, it ___ (melt).
checks.explanation: For a general truth, both clauses use the present simple (zero conditional).

sections.title: Second conditional
sections.summary: Use the second conditional for unreal or unlikely situations in the present or future, and for advice.

tables.caption: Structure of the second conditional
head: if clause
main clause
rows: we would see her more often.

uses: An unreal or very unlikely situation: If I won the lottery, I would buy a house.
Advice, with if I were you: If I were you, I would take the job.
Use were for all persons in a formal style: If he were taller, he would play basketball.

examples.text: If I had a car, I would drive to work.
What would you do if you lost your passport?
If I were you, I would talk to the teacher.
examples.note: A common way to give advice.

mistakes.wrong: If I would have time, I would help you.
mistakes.right: If I had time, I would help you.
mistakes.why: Do not use would in the if clause. Use the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: If I was rich, I will buy a boat.
mistakes.right: If I were rich, I would buy a boat.
mistakes.why: The main clause needs would, not will, for an unreal situation.

checks.question: Complete: If I ___ (know) the answer, I would tell you.
checks.explanation: The if clause uses the past simple, but the meaning is present.

checks.question: Complete: She ___ (travel) more if she had more money.
checks.explanation: The main clause of the second conditional uses would plus the base form.

sections.title: Third conditional
sections.summary: Use the third conditional to talk about an unreal past: something that did not happen and what the result would have been.

tables.caption: Structure of the third conditional
head: if clause
main clause
rows: I would have passed the exam.
she would not have missed the train.

uses: Imagine a different past: If we had taken a taxi, we would have arrived on time.
Express regret: If I had listened to you, I would not have made that mistake.
Express relief or criticism: If you had told me, I would have helped.
Could have and might have are possible in the main clause: If he had asked, I might have said yes.

examples.text: If it had not rained, we would have gone to the beach.
What would you have done if you had missed the flight?
If I had known about the party, I would have come.

mistakes.wrong: If I would have known, I would have told you.
mistakes.right: If I had known, I would have told you.
mistakes.why: Use the past perfect in the if clause, not would have.

mistakes.wrong: If she had studied, she would passed.
mistakes.right: If she had studied, she would have passed.
mistakes.why: The main clause needs would have plus the past participle.

checks.question: Complete: If I ___ (see) the sign, I would have stopped.
checks.explanation: Past perfect in the if clause.

checks.question: Complete: If they had invited me, I ___ (go).
checks.explanation: Would have plus the past participle.

sections.title: Mixed conditionals
sections.summary: Mix the second and third conditional when the time in the if clause is different from the time in the result.

tables.caption: Two common mixed patterns
head: pattern
if clause
main clause
example
rows: If I had taken that job, I would be rich now.
If I were more careful, I would not have broken it.

uses: A past action that has a result now: If she had gone to university, she would have a better job today.
A permanent present situation that explains a past event: If he were not so shy, he would have spoken to her.
Look for time words such as now, today, still and yesterday to choose the correct form.

examples.text: If I had saved more, I would be on holiday now.
If they were not so busy, they would have come to the party.
If you had told me, I would know what to do.

mistakes.wrong: If I had more money, I would have bought it yesterday.
mistakes.right: If I had had more money, I would have bought it yesterday.
mistakes.why: Use the past perfect when the condition is in the past.

mistakes.wrong: If he would be here now, he had helped.
mistakes.right: If he were here now, he would help.
mistakes.why: Do not use would in the if clause.

checks.question: Complete: If I had slept well, I ___ (not be) so tired now.
Complete: If she ___ (be) more patient, she would not have shouted.
checks.explanation: Present condition (she is not patient), past result.

sections.title: Wishes: wish and if only
sections.summary: Use wish and if only to talk about things you would like to be different.

tables.caption: Wish and if only
head: about
verb form
example
rows: I wish I had a bigger flat.
I wish I had studied harder.
a future change or annoying habit
I wish you would stop shouting.

uses: Present regrets use the past simple: I wish I lived near the sea.
Use were for all persons in a formal style: I wish I were taller.
Past regrets use the past perfect: If only I had listened to her.
Wish + would is for something that annoys you. You cannot use it about yourself.
If only is stronger than wish: If only I knew the answer!

examples.text: I wish I could play the piano.
If only we had left earlier!
I wish it would stop raining.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I have more time.
mistakes.right: I wish I had more time.
mistakes.why: The present wish needs the past simple.

mistakes.wrong: I wish I would be taller.
mistakes.why: Do not use wish + would about yourself.

checks.question: Complete: I wish I ___ (know) his number.
checks.explanation: A present wish uses the past simple.

checks.question: Complete: If only I ___ (take) the earlier train.
checks.explanation: A past regret uses the past perfect.

sections.title: Unless, as long as and other words
sections.summary: Other words can replace if in the first conditional and add a different meaning.

tables.caption: Words that can replace if
head: word
meaning
example
rows: I will go unless it rains.
You can borrow it as long as you return it.
Take an umbrella in case it rains.
Hurry up, otherwise we will be late.

uses: Unless already has a negative meaning. Do not add not after it.
As long as and provided that set a condition: I will help provided that you ask.
In case is about preparing for a problem, not about a condition for the action.
Use the present simple after these words, not will.

examples.text: We will have the picnic unless the weather is bad.
You can stay here as long as you are quiet.
Take some water in case you get thirsty.
examples.note: You take it before the problem.

mistakes.wrong: Unless you do not hurry, you will be late.
mistakes.right: Unless you hurry, you will be late.
mistakes.why: Unless means if not. A second negative is wrong.

mistakes.wrong: I will call you in case I will need help.
mistakes.right: I will call you in case I need help.
mistakes.why: Use the present simple after in case.

checks.question: Choose: I will go out (unless / if) it rains.
checks.explanation: The meaning is: if it does not rain.

checks.question: Choose: Take a jacket (in case / unless) it gets cold.
checks.explanation: You take the jacket to be ready for a problem.
